definition: Statistical machine translation (SMT) is a machine translation approach where translations are generated on the basis of statistical models whose parameters are derived from the analysis of bilingual text corpora.
details: The statistical approach contrasts with the rule-based approaches to machine translation as well as with example-based machine translation, that superseded the previous rule-based approach that required explicit description of each and every linguistic rule, which was costly, and which often did not generalize to other languages. The first ideas of statistical machine translation were introduced by Warren Weaver in 1949, including the ideas of applying Claude Shannon's information theory. Statistical machine translation was re-introduced in the late 1980s and early 1990s by researchers at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center. Before the introduction of neural machine translation, it was by far the most widely studied machine translation method.

explainer.lead: Statistical machine translation generates translations using statistical models whose parameters come from bilingual text corpora. It matters because it replaced costly hand-written linguistic rules.

tiers.eli5: Instead of writing grammar rules by hand, the system learns how words and phrases pair up by reading lots of translated text.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers train models on parallel corpora rather than encoding rules per language. A pitfall is that rule-based systems often failed to generalize, and SMT in turn was superseded by example-based approaches.
tiers.paperLevel: Translations are produced from statistical models with parameters derived from analysis of bilingual text corpora, contrasting with rule-based and example-based translation. Warren Weaver introduced the ideas in 1949, including applying Shannon's information theory.

explainer.example: A system learns phrase pairs from a large bilingual corpus and scores candidate translations from those learned statistics.
